analysis.one_liner: Raises the bar for courts to let the government seize your online records in secret, and forces eventual notice to you.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 412-0 with no votes against in May 2023, but the Senate never voted, and it died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When police want your emails, texts, or cloud files, they send a legal demand to the company holding them. The company is usually allowed to tell you — but the government can ask a judge for a secrecy order that forbids it, sometimes for months. This bill would make those secrecy orders much harder to get: a judge would have to put specific written findings on the record, the order could only last 90 days at a time, and once it expired the government would have to tell you and give you a copy of whatever was handed over. It would also let the company challenge the order in court and would force the Justice Department to report every year on how often it uses this power, including against journalists. The House passed it with no votes against; the Senate never acted.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose emails, texts, or cloud records the government seeks — they would learn the demand existed once secrecy ended, see exactly what was handed over, and the secrecy itself would require a judge to put specific written findings on the record first. Journalists and people engaged in protected political activity get an annual accounting of how often the government targets them. The companies holding the records (email and cloud providers) gain the right to go to court to challenge a secrecy order and to consult a lawyer about it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone targeted by secret records demands

how_it_helps.text: It raises the standard: a judge can only let the government keep a records demand secret by issuing a written determination, based on specific facts, that secrecy is likely needed to prevent danger to life, flight, evidence destruction, witness intimidation, or serious jeopardy to an investigation.
It caps the secrecy at 90 days at a time, requires the order to be narrowly tailored with no less restrictive alternative, and requires the government to tell the court if circumstances change.

Once the secrecy order expires, the government must notify the target by at least two methods, tell them what information was handed over, and provide a copy of the disclosed information on request within 180 days.
It lets the provider that received the order go to court to challenge or modify it, and stay disclosure while the challenge is pending, and it lets the provider share the order with a lawyer.

It requires the Justice Department to report annually, by judicial district, on how many people were targeted, how many secrecy orders were granted or denied, how many affected news media members or First Amendment activity, and what arrests and convictions resulted.

analysis.who_pays: Federal law enforcement and prosecutors, who lose the easy ability to keep records demands secret from their targets and must now give notice, written findings, and copies of disclosed information, plus file annual reports. In concrete cases, an investigation where a target would otherwise never learn of the records seizure now ends with the target being notified.

drawbacks.text: Raising the standard for secrecy could hinder undercover investigations. Law enforcement argues delayed notice is essential when tipping off a target would let evidence be destroyed, witnesses be intimidated, or suspects flee; the bill narrows how easily judges can grant that secrecy and caps each order at 90 days.

The bill requires the government to notify the target after the secrecy order expires and to provide a copy of what was disclosed, which reveals the existence of an investigation even when the person investigated was never charged or was cleared.
Giving providers the right to challenge orders in court and to stay disclosure while the challenge is pending adds litigation and delay to cases where prosecutors believe speed matters.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real: today the government can get records about you from a tech company and the company can be ordered never to tell you, under a standard that does not require the judge to write down why. The bill replaces that with specific written findings, short time limits, mandatory notice afterward, a copy of what was taken, and public annual reporting — meaningful privacy protections that also make the government accountable for how often it uses this tool. The cost is honest: investigators argue that secrecy is sometimes essential to keep people alive, keep witnesses safe, or keep evidence from being destroyed, and the bill's tighter written-findings requirement and mandatory expiration notice could complicate some undercover cases, even with the life-safety and flight exceptions preserved. On balance the protections outweigh the costs, since the bill still permits secrecy whenever a judge finds specific danger, but the objection is genuine and not merely procedural.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it unanimously, but the Senate Judiciary Committee never voted on it before the two-year Congress ended, so it just died.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced May 5, 2023, and cleared the House Judiciary Committee on a voice vote within a week.
On May 15, 2023, the House passed it 412-0 under a fast-track procedure requiring a two-thirds majority, with 200 of 216 Democrats and 212 of 224 Republicans voting yes and no one voting no.
The Senate received the bill on May 16, 2023, and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, which took no further action for the remaining twenty months of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal investigators are better off, since the looser rules for secretly seizing records and delaying notice to targets remain in place; the tech providers that prefer quietly complying with government demands also keep the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal investigators; the status quo held

for.name: Scott Fitzgerald
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and moved to suspend the rules and pass it, bringing it to a House vote within ten days of introduction.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a markup five days after introduction, ordered the bill reported by voice vote, and reported it with a written report.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Senate committee where the bill sat
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 16, 2023, and referred it to committee, then took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration in the twenty months after the House passed it.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote was unanimous: 200 of 216 Democrats and 212 of 224 Republicans voted yes, with zero no votes in either party.

industries.note: The bill gives these companies new tools: the right to go to court to challenge or modify a secrecy order, the ability to pause disclosure while a challenge is pending, and the ability to consult a lawyer about the order. Their interest here runs alongside their customers', since both want fewer unchallengeable secret demands.

Investigators lose easy access to long, lightly-scrutinized secrecy orders and must give targets notice and copies of the records after secrecy ends. This is the intended cost: the bill constrains a government power that currently operates largely without the target ever knowing.
